Debt can affect every part of your life, from your credit score to your peace of mind. Knowing your legal options is essential if you’re struggling to make payments, dealing with debt collectors, or trying to protect your home or car.

Chapter 13 bankruptcy is a way to manage debt without losing your assets immediately. Unlike Chapter 7 bankruptcy, which involves selling assets to pay off debt, Chapter 13 lets you create a repayment plan. This plan usually lasts three to five years and is based on your income and ability to pay.

In this article, we’ll explain how Chapter 13 works, who qualifies, and how it compares to Chapter 7. We’ll also cover why some people switch between the two and the responsibilities of filing for Chapter 13. Understanding the benefits and limitations lets you decide if this option is right for your financial situation.

If you’re thinking about bankruptcy, learning about Chapter 13 is a good place to start. It can help you make an informed and confident decision.

Understanding Chapter 13 Bankruptcy

Chapter 13 bankruptcy, also called a “wage earner’s plan,” helps individuals with regular income repay their debts over three to five years under a plan approved by the court. Unlike Chapter 7 bankruptcy, which involves selling your assets to pay creditors, Chapter 13 lets you keep your property while catching up on overdue payments.

Here’s how Chapter 13 works:

  • Repayment Plan: You propose a repayment plan to the court that prioritizes certain debts. This includes overdue payments on secured debts (like mortgages or car loans), priority debts (such as taxes or child support), and potentially part of your unsecured debts (like credit cards). The plan must follow specific legal rules outlined in 11 U.S.C. § 1322.
  • Automatic Stay: When you file, the court immediately issues an automatic stay that stops most collection actions, including lawsuits, wage garnishments, and creditor calls.
  • Keeping Your Property: You can keep your home, car, and other assets as long as you adhere to the repayment plan and make the required payments.
  • Income-Based Payments: Your monthly payment is based on your disposable income, which the court reviews to ensure it is reasonable and follows the law under 11 U.S.C. § 1325.
  • Catching Up on Missed Payments: If you’ve fallen behind on secured debts, like a car loan or mortgage, you can include the overdue amounts in your repayment plan and pay them off gradually. This often prevents repossession or foreclosure.

Chapter 13 also includes tools to reduce or modify debts:

  • Cramdowns: Reduce the amount you owe on secured debts to match the asset’s current value (like a car).
  • Lien Stripping: Remove junior liens, such as second mortgages, if certain conditions are met.

However, not everyone qualifies for Chapter 13. You’ll need a steady income and must meet debt limits outlined in 11 U.S.C. § 109. It’s a structured process that requires careful planning and strict compliance with the repayment plan.

If you’re considering Chapter 13, start by reviewing your debts, income, and financial goals to determine if it’s the right solution for your situation.

What Is Chapter 7 Bankruptcy?

Chapter 7 bankruptcy, often called “liquidation bankruptcy,” is a legal process that helps individuals eliminate most unsecured debts. It’s governed by Chapter 7 of the U.S. Bankruptcy Code and is supervised by a court. Key details include:

  • Review of Assets and Exemptions: A court-appointed trustee will review your assets to see if any non-essential property can be sold to repay creditors. However, most people keep essential items like household goods, a personal vehicle, or their primary home, thanks to federal or Iowa state exemptions under 11 U.S.C. § 522.
  • Discharge of Debts: If approved, the court will erase most unsecured debts, such as credit card balances, medical bills, and personal loans, under 11 U.S.C. § 727. However, some debts, like recent taxes, child support, and student loans, cannot typically be discharged.
  • Means Test Eligibility: Your income must pass the means test outlined in 11 U.S.C. § 707(b) to qualify. This compares your income to the median income for a household of your size in Iowa. If your income is too high, you must file under Chapter 13 instead.
  • Timeline for Completion: Most Chapter 7 cases are resolved in three to six months, making it a quick option for debt relief.
  • Impact on Credit: A Chapter 7 bankruptcy stays on your credit report for up to 10 years, but many people rebuild their credit soon after their case is discharged.

Chapter 7 bankruptcy offers a fresh financial start for eligible individuals. Before filing, it is essential to understand how exemptions, discharge rules, and income requirements apply to your situation.

Reasons to Convert from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7

Sometimes, a Chapter 13 repayment plan doesn’t work out as expected. A drop in income, unexpected expenses, or changing household needs can make it hard to keep up with payments. In such cases, switching to Chapter 7 bankruptcy could be a better option if you meet the legal qualifications, such as passing the means test.

Some key reasons to convert include:

  • Faster Debt Relief: Chapter 13 repayment plans take 3 to 5 years to complete, while Chapter 7 cases typically wrap up in just a few months, providing quicker relief from most unsecured debts.
  • No More Monthly Payments: In Chapter 13, you must make regular payments to a trustee. Chapter 7 eliminates this requirement for most debts, freeing up room in your budget.
  • More straightforward Process: Chapter 7 involves fewer court filings and no need to adjust repayment plans, making it a more straightforward option for those with limited income or few assets.

Here are a few things to consider before converting:

  • Eligibility: To switch to Chapter 7, you must pass the means test, which checks if your income is low enough to qualify. You may not be allowed to convert if your income is too high.
  • Impact on Assets: Chapter 13 protects assets by allowing you to repay debts over time. In Chapter 7, non-exempt property could be sold to pay creditors. However, state or federal exemptions may help protect certain assets.
  • Secured Debts: If you’re behind on payments for things like a mortgage or car loan, Chapter 7 doesn’t allow you to catch up on missed payments like Chapter 13 does. This issue with secured debts could risk your home, car, or other collateral.

Before deciding to convert, examine your financial situation, including your income, debts, and assets. Converting without careful consideration could affect your ability to protect your property or qualify for a discharge. Speak with a bankruptcy attorney to ensure this is the right move for your circumstances.

Other Potential Drawbacks of Converting to Chapter 7

While Chapter 7 can offer tremendous relief from burdensome debt, it’s essential to consider the drawbacks before you initiate a conversion:

  • Risk of Losing Assets: Depending on your situation, certain non-exempt assets might be sold to help pay your creditors. Iowa’s exemption laws protect much of your essential property, but it’s crucial to discuss specifics, especially if you own valuable items or significant equity in your home.
  • Eligibility Restrictions: You must pass the means test to qualify for Chapter 7. You might not be eligible to convert if your income is too high. We’ll help you determine whether you meet this requirement.
  • Long-Term Credit Impact: Because Chapter 7 remains on your credit report for up to 10 years, you’ll need to commit to rebuilding your credit over time. Many of our clients still find that the immediate financial freedom outweighs the credit implications.
  • Certain Debts Not Discharged: Chapter 7 generally doesn’t eliminate student loans, most taxes, and child support obligations. We’ll examine your full debt picture to paint a realistic view of what can and can’t be wiped out.

It’s also worth noting that some people hesitate about filing for bankruptcy due to fear or perceived stigma. However, taking proactive steps to resolve debt is a mark of strength, not failure. By choosing to explore your options—whether that means staying in Chapter 13 or moving to Chapter 7—you’re prioritizing your family’s well-being and your own peace of mind.

How a Bankruptcy Attorney Can Help

When you decide that converting from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 might be the best option, here’s what you can expect:

  1. Evaluating Your Situation: We’ll review your current Chapter 13 repayment plan and overall financial picture. This includes your monthly income, living expenses, total debt, and any significant changes since you filed for Chapter 13.
  2. Filing the Motion to Convert: If conversion is in your best interest, we’ll file a Motion to Convert with the bankruptcy court, formally requesting the shift from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.
  3. Submitting New Documents: You must update your financial forms, including your income and expenses, so the court can confirm that you qualify for and understand Chapter 7 requirements.
  4. Attending a New 341 Meeting: Once your case is converted, you’ll attend another creditors’ meeting. This is an opportunity for the trustee and any creditors to ask questions about your finances.
  5. Addressing Your Assets: The court-appointed trustee will evaluate which assets may be exempt and which may not. We’ll strategize with you to protect as much of your property as possible, using both federal and state exemptions.

If you have concerns about timing, reasonable faith requirements, or objections from creditors or trustees, our Henkels & Baker, PC team will work through them together. Our goal is to make the entire bankruptcy filing process clear, efficient, and aligned with your long-term interests.

Determining If Conversion Is Right for You

Converting from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 isn’t just a matter of filling out paperwork. It’s a big decision that can drastically change your financial path. If you’re wondering whether it’s the right move, here are a few signs that Chapter 7 might be more suitable:

  • You’re struggling to keep up with the requirements of your Chapter 13 plan.
  • Your income has dropped, or you’ve encountered new bills that make consistent payments difficult.
  • You feel like you need a faster route to debt discharge, instead of waiting several years.
  • You lack significant non-exempt assets that a Chapter 7 trustee could sell.

We always start by discussing your immediate needs and long-term goals. Sometimes, remaining in Chapter 13 or seeking a plan modification makes sense. Other times, conversion can be a lifeline, opening the door to a fresh start sooner rather than later.

If you’re feeling overwhelmed, remember that our office is a judgment-free zone. You deserve to feel empowered about your financial future, and we’re here to guide you.
